questions.question_text: Which one of these is a unit vector?

options.why: This arrow is $7$ units long, so its magnitude is $7$, not $1$.
This arrow is $7$ units long, so its magnitude is $7$, not $1$.
The zero vector has magnitude $0$; a unit vector must have magnitude exactly $1$.

questions.solution_text:
$-\underset{\sim}{i}$ is $\underset{\sim}{i}$ turned round, so it is $1$ unit long pointing to the left.
$|-\underset{\sim}{i}|=1$
A unit vector may point in any direction, so $-\underset{\sim}{i}$ is the unit vector.

questions.question_text:
$\underset{\sim}{p}$ is a non-zero vector.
Which expression is equal to $\underset{\sim}{0}$?

options.why: Adding a vector to itself doubles its length, giving $2\underset{\sim}{p}$.
Multiplying by $1$ leaves the vector unchanged; only multiplying by $0$ gives the zero vector.
The minus sign reverses the direction but keeps the magnitude, so the result is not the zero vector.

questions.solution_text:
Subtracting a vector from itself leaves no length at all.
$\underset{\sim}{p}-\underset{\sim}{p}=\underset{\sim}{0}$

questions.question_text: On a grid, what movement does $6\underset{\sim}{j}$ describe?

options.why: $\underset{\sim}{j}$ points up, so only $-6\underset{\sim}{j}$ would go down.
Used $\underset{\sim}{i}$, the horizontal unit vector, instead of $\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Swapped $\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $\underset{\sim}{i}$ and reversed the sign as well.

questions.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{j}$ is a move of $1$ unit up.
The scalar $6$ makes the move six times as long in the same direction.
$6\underset{\sim}{j}$ is a move of $6$ units up.

questions.question_text: Which statement about the zero vector $\underset{\sim}{0}$ is correct?

options.text: It has magnitude $0$ and no direction.
It has magnitude $0$ and points in every direction.
options.why: A vector has one direction at most; the zero vector has none at all.

options.text: It has magnitude $1$ and no direction.
options.why: Confuses the zero vector with a unit vector, which has magnitude $1$.

options.text: It is the same as the number $0$.
options.why: The zero vector is a vector and $0$ is a scalar, so the two are different kinds of quantity.

questions.solution_text:
An arrow of magnitude $0$ has its head and its tail in the same place.
That leaves a single point with no arrowhead, so no direction can be read from it.
The zero vector has magnitude $0$ and no direction.

questions.question_text:
On a diagram where $1$ cm represents $1$ unit, $\underset{\sim}{s}$ is drawn as an arrow $0.2$ cm long.
Which statement is correct?

options.text: $\underset{\sim}{s}$ is not a unit vector, because its magnitude is $0.2$ and not $1$.
$\underset{\sim}{s}$ is a unit vector, because it is short.
options.why: Being short does not make a vector a unit vector; the magnitude must be exactly $1$.

options.text: $\underset{\sim}{s}$ is the zero vector, because it is so short.
options.why: Only an arrow of magnitude $0$ is the zero vector, and this arrow has a length and a direction.

options.text: $\underset{\sim}{s}$ is not a vector at all, because it is too short to show a direction.
options.why: Any arrow with a length and a direction is a vector, however short it is drawn.

questions.solution_text:
The arrow is $0.2$ cm long and $1$ cm stands for $1$ unit.
$|\underset{\sim}{s}|=0.2$
A unit vector needs magnitude exactly $1$, so $\underset{\sim}{s}$ is not a unit vector.

options.why: $\underset{\sim}{a}$ spans $3$ squares, so its magnitude is $3$.
$\underset{\sim}{c}$ spans $2$ squares, so its magnitude is $2$.

questions.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{b}$ spans exactly one grid square, so it is $1$ unit long.
$|\underset{\sim}{b}|=1$
$\underset{\sim}{b}$ is the unit vector.

questions.question_text: Which statement about $\underset{\sim}{i}$ and $\underset{\sim}{j}$ is correct?

options.text: They are perpendicular and each has magnitude $1$.
They are parallel and each has magnitude $1$.
options.why: $\underset{\sim}{i}$ runs across and $\underset{\sim}{j}$ runs up, so they meet at a right angle.

options.text: They are perpendicular and each has magnitude $2$.
options.why: Each basis vector is one unit long, not two.

options.text: They are parallel and each has magnitude $2$.
options.why: Both parts are wrong: the basis vectors are perpendicular and each is one unit long.

questions.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{i}$ points $1$ unit along the $x$-axis and $\underset{\sim}{j}$ points $1$ unit along the $y$-axis.
The axes meet at a right angle, so the two vectors are perpendicular.
They are perpendicular and each has magnitude $1$.

questions.question_text:
A hiker walks from camp $C$ to lookout $L$, then walks straight back to $C$.
Which vector describes the displacement for the whole walk?

options.why: Gives the first leg only and ignores the walk back.
Adds the two legs as lengths, ignoring that the return leg points the opposite way.
That is the distance to the lookout, a scalar, not the displacement of the whole walk.

questions.solution_text:
The walk out is $\overrightarrow{CL}$ and the walk back is $\overrightarrow{LC}=-\overrightarrow{CL}$.
$\overrightarrow{CL}-\overrightarrow{CL}$
$=\underset{\sim}{0}$, because the hiker finishes at the point where the walk began.
